The first result presented here is a comparison of the results from integrating the simulation using the distances versus a more traditional time based integration. A summary of the results from one simulation evaluated using the distance and time integration, as presented in the web interface, is shown in Fig. 4. For this example, a route from Chicago to Cleveland is chosen. The consist includes 1 diesel and 2 smaller battery locomotives pulling 50 loaded tank cars. A naive powering policy using diesel then battery power, maximum braking, and a maximum speed of 60 mph is used. The relative energy flows from each source is shown in the bar chart. The regenerated energy is the amount of energy recovered and made available to the batteries to use. 7 Fig. 4 Comparison of results summary from E-LTD distance and time integrations Detailed results from a single, distance based simulation are shown in Fig. 5. The top plot is a summary of how power is distributed along the route. The second plot shows the maximum, target, and actual speeds for the consist. The third plot shows the elevation, giving the user some evidence for the variations in the energy flows in the first plot. Finally, the last plot shows the charge state of the batteries. It gives the user an indication of where the battery runs out of charge and the amount of charge that was regenerated and used again throughout the route. Fig. 5 Detailed Results of E-LTD distance integration One of the key observations of using the naïve policy is we prematurely drain the battery energy and can no longer sustain the target speeds for significant portions of the route. We next explore the results from using the optimal policy. A summary of the results for the same consist on the same route as demonstrated above is shown in Fig. 6. The initial setting for the optimal policy is to use a maximum speed of 60 mph. The algorithm determines that it is not feasible to travel that fast with the power and stored energy available in the current consist as is described in the previous section. The algorithm determines a feasible maximum speed of 8 49.6 mph, 10 mph slower than the naïve policy. The key results are the overall transit time is still reduced from 6.62 hrs to 6.22 hrs and the total fuel consumed is also reduced from 4599 kg to 4485 kg. The detailed results for the simulation using the optimal policy are shown in Fig. 7. On first glance, there is a significant difference in the amount of regeneration occurring throughout the route. With the manual policy shown in Fig. 5, regeneration only occurs during braking situations. When using the optimal policy, when power capacity is available, it is used to charge the batteries, providing more available energy in regions of the route that require more power to sustain the target speed or to reduce the time to increase consist speed to the current target
